title: the Manusmriti — read critically
hook: two quote cards, both signed Manu, that seem to say opposite things
tomorrow: is varna in Manu decided by birth, or by how you live?

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Manusmriti's page for distress: a starving sage, and a chandala who argued back. Read the edges. Today, two lines from the middle.

A pretty quote card goes around a feed, gold letters on pink: where women are honored, there the gods rejoice. Signed, Manu. A few posts down, someone answers with another line, also signed Manu: a woman is not fit for independence. People pile in on both sides. Here's the odd part. Both lines are real, and they come from the same book. So which one is the Manusmriti?
screen: `A QUOTE CARD: WOMEN HONORED.` → `A REPLY: NOT FIT FOR INDEPENDENCE.` → `SAME BOOK?`

segments.voice: Here they are, in paraphrase. Chapter three: where women are honored, the gods rejoice; where they are not, every rite bears no fruit. The Sanskrit is often quoted, yatra naryastu pujyante. Chapter nine: her father guards her in childhood, her husband in youth, her sons in old age; a woman is not fit for independence. The puzzle starts to come apart when you read each line in its own chapter. The honoring verse sits in a passage about the household. Fathers, brothers, husbands and brothers-in-law are told to honor and adorn the women of the family, and the book warns that a family where the women grieve soon falls apart. The guarding verse sits in a passage on husbands and wives. Put side by side, they make one picture: women are to be honored, inside the family's protection, and not on their own. In this book, honor and freedom are not the same word. Readers take that in different ways. Some hold the honoring verse as the heart of it and set the other down. Some scholars read the book as layers, gathered over time. And critics quote the guarding verse to show what the book asked of women's lives. Here's the move to keep. A quote card is one line. A book is the whole page. Read the chapter before you share the verse, whichever verse it is.
screen: `CHAPTER THREE: HONORED.` · `CHAPTER NINE: GUARDED, NOT FREE.` · `HONOR IS NOT FREEDOM HERE.` · then, large: `READ THE WHOLE PAGE.`

segments.voice: If there's paper near you, write the name of a woman who taught you something, and under it, the one thing she taught. Then rest your eyes on what you wrote, and read it again on each slow out-breath until the bell.
The Manusmriti: a book where women are honored in one chapter and kept from independence in another.
Hold on to it: the Manusmriti, read critically, the whole page before the one line. Back tomorrow.

howItsDone: The line 'yatra naryastu pujyante' is often quoted on its own at weddings, in speeches and on posters; teachers who read the Manusmriti critically set it beside the chapter-nine verse on guarding women and read both in context.

fork.setup: a cousin's wedding speech will quote 'where women are honored, the gods rejoice.' an aunt asks you: is that all Manu says about women? what's the honest answer?
options: it's real, and the same book also limits women. both are in it.
yes, that line is the book's whole view of women.
no, that line was never in Manu at all.
fork.reveal: chapter three honors; chapter nine guards and limits. the line can be said at a wedding, and the honest answer names both.

original.note: Sanskrit, Manusmriti 3.56: where women are honored. the verse goes on: there the gods rejoice.

trapdoor: what you thought: Manu is either all honor for women or all control.
what it means: both are in it, honor in chapter three and guarding in chapter nine, one picture of women inside the family.
what a scholar hears: 3.56 'yatra naryastu pujyante' beside 9.3 'na stri svatantryam arhati'; some scholars read the text as gathered in layers.
guess: an old law book that both honors and limits women
a book of hymns to the goddesses of the home
a modern code of rights for Hindu women
recall: dharma in distress: rules bend for a life
a starving sage; the chandala argued back

chat.says: found the perfect clap-back: 'where women are honored, the gods rejoice.' posting it. thoughts??
options: it's real, but the same book says she's not fit for independence. quote both.
post it. that verse settles what Manu thinks about women, full stop.
don't. it's a modern saying, and it isn't in the Manusmriti at all.
chat.meaning: Both lines are in the Manusmriti, chapters three and nine. Honored, yet not independent: reading critically means the whole page, not one card.

Manusmriti.meaning: an old Sanskrit law book, the dharma teaching of Manu

Manu.meaning: the lawgiver tradition names as the book's speaker

yatra naryastu pujyante.meaning: where women are honored: the start of Manusmriti 3.56

sources.ref: Manusmriti 3.55–3.58 (women of the family to be honored and adorned; where women are honored the gods rejoice, 3.56; a family where women grieve soon perishes, 3.57)
Manusmriti 9.2–9.3 (father, husband and sons guard a woman; a woman is not fit for independence)

notes: Puzzle shape: the odd detail is two quotable lines from one book that seem to clash; solved by reading each in its chapter. Answers 1569's question.

Manu 3.56 ('yatra nāryas tu pūjyante ramante tatra devatāḥ / yatraitās tu na pūjyante sarvās tatrāphalāḥ kriyāḥ') and 9.3 ('pitā rakṣati kaumāre bhartā rakṣati yauvane / rakṣanti sthavire putrā na strī svātantryam arhati') are paraphrased; the voice uses no quotation marks. The same idea is also at 5.147–148. Confirm.
'Some scholars read the book as layers, gathered over time' is a soft attribution (e.g. discussions of the text's composition); no dates or names given. Confirm or name.
'Critics quote the guarding verse to show what the book asked of women's lives' is deliberately unnamed and unquantified.
